formation.title: The Restoration of Al-Andalus
formation.text:
The crescent banner flies once more over all of Iberia. Where Christian kingdoms once carved up the peninsula, a united Islamic state has risen from the ashes of the taifas. The memory of the Caliphate of Cordoba, when this land was the most learned and prosperous in all of Europe, burns bright in every scholar and soldier.

But Al-Andalus faces a choice that has defined it since the days of the Umayyads. Will we revive the tradition of the convivencia, where mosques stood beside synagogues and churches, where Ibn Rushd debated Aristotle and Maimonides found refuge under Muslim rule? Or will we follow the path of the Almohads and Almoravids, who crossed the strait with armies of disciplined Berber cavalry and built an empire through military piety and religious orthodoxy?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: Let Cordoba shine again as the ornament of the world.

modifiers.name: Ornament of the World
modifiers.text: Al-Andalus shines as a beacon of learning where Muslim, Christian, and Jewish scholars exchange knowledge freely, and the libraries of Cordoba rival any in the world.

options.text: The sword of the Maghreb shall unite the faithful.

modifiers.name: Sword of the Maghreb
modifiers.text: Forged in the fires of jihad, the warriors of Al-Andalus march beneath the banner of a purified faith, their Berber cavalry and frontier ghazis striking fear across the peninsula.

advances.name: Zanata Horsemanship
advances.text: The riders of Al-Andalus learned their craft from the Zanata Berbers who crossed the Strait to serve its rulers: short stirrups, a light saddle, and javelins hurled from the saddle at full gallop.

advances.name: Ribat Frontier Defense
advances.text: The ribats guard the borders of the faithful, combining fortress walls with monastic discipline.

advances.name: Acequia Irrigation
advances.text: The acequia canal systems of Al-Andalus transform arid land into gardens, applying centuries of Islamic hydraulic knowledge.

advances.name: Maliki Jurists of Cordoba
advances.text: The legal scholars of Al-Andalus develop a sophisticated tradition of fiqh, drawing on the Maliki school to create orderly governance.

advances.name: Urban Civilization
advances.text: The cities of Al-Andalus set the standard for urban life, with public baths, paved streets, and running water.

advances.name: Mosque Network
advances.text: A network of congregational mosques anchors religious life across Al-Andalus, from the Great Mosque of Cordoba to humble village houses of prayer.

advances.name: Zenata Horse Guard
advances.text: Elite Berber cavalry from the Zenata tribes form the core of the Andalusi heavy horse, disciplined and fearsome in the charge.

advances.name: Schools of al-Hakam
advances.text: The caliph al-Hakam II opened twenty-seven schools in Cordoba where the children of the poor were taught without fee by masters on his payroll. Andalusi masters begin with Arabic, verse and a fair hand before the Qur'an, as Ibn Khaldun noted of them.

advances.name: Qirad Partnerships
advances.text: An investor entrusts money or goods to a merchant, who sails with them and brings back a share of the profit. The contract is drawn up by the notaries of the town from the formularies of Cordoba, and it lets Andalusi capital travel farther than its owners.

advances.name: Equals of the Arabs
advances.text: Ibn Gharsiya, a Basque convert at the court of Denia, wrote in the 1050s that the peoples the Arabs had conquered were their equals, and their betters in learning. Berbers, Slavs and the converted natives of the peninsula hold office beside the old Arab families.

event.title: The Letter from Denia
event.text:
A letter is passing from hand to hand among the secretaries. Its author is Ibn Gharsiya, born a Basque Christian, taken as a child and raised a Muslim, now a poet at the court of Denia. He writes that the Arabs are masters at describing camels, and that philosophy, astronomy and the measuring of the earth belong to the peoples they conquered. Seven scholars have written replies. Nobody has asked for his head.

The quarrel is an old one in Al-Andalus. Berbers carried the conquest, Slavs commanded the palace guard and the sons of converted natives fill the chanceries, yet the old Arab families still count a man's descent before they count his learning. A realm that means to hold the whole peninsula cannot afford the habit.

options.text: A man is what he knows.

modifiers.name: Scholars of Every Nation
modifiers.text: Berber, Slav, convert and Arab are judged by what they know. The courts of Al-Andalus fill with scholars of every origin.

advances.name: Naval Arsenal
advances.text: The dar al-sina'a of Almeria and Algeciras produce war galleys that command the western Mediterranean.

advances.name: Governors of the Kuras
advances.text: The Umayyads divided Al-Andalus into kuras, each under a governor named and recalled by Cordoba, and into three marches under commanders on the frontier. Tax registers and judges answer to the capital, not to the governor.

advances.name: Ghazi Warriors
advances.text: The ghazis of Al-Andalus are frontier warriors who combine religious zeal with battlefield prowess, defending the Dar al-Islam.

effects.name: Damage Done versus Heathens in Battle

advances.name: Alcazar Fortification
advances.text: The alcazars of Al-Andalus are fortified palace complexes that serve as seats of power and bastions of defense.

advances.name: Translation Movement
advances.text: The systematic translation of Arabic scholarly works into Latin and Hebrew transforms Al-Andalus into the intellectual bridge between Islamic and Christian civilizations, while lusterware ceramics showcase the material culture born from this exchange.

event.title: The Translation Movement
event.text:
The translation houses of Al-Andalus have become the intellectual crossroads of the world. In Toledo, Cordoba, and Seville, Arabic texts on medicine, astronomy, mathematics, and philosophy are being rendered into Latin, Hebrew, and Romance languages. The works of al-Zahrawi on surgery, al-Zarqali on astronomical instruments, and Ibn Rushd on Aristotelian philosophy are reshaping the intellectual landscape far beyond the borders of the Islamic world.

But a question divides our scholars. Should we preserve our intellectual tradition in its Arabic purity, continuing to produce original works that advance human knowledge? Or should we embrace the role of universal translator, making all knowledge accessible across linguistic and religious boundaries, even at the cost of diluting our distinctive scholarly identity?

options.text: Our tradition speaks for itself: let us build upon it.

modifiers.name: Arabic Scholarly Tradition
modifiers.text: Al-Andalus preserves and extends the Arabic intellectual tradition, producing original works that stand alongside the greatest achievements of Baghdad and Cairo.

modifiers.name: Universal Knowledge Exchange
modifiers.text: The translation houses of Al-Andalus serve as a bridge between civilizations, transmitting the wisdom of the ancients to all who would learn.

advances.name: Silk Industry
advances.text: The silk workshops of Granada and Almeria produce the finest textiles in Europe, their damasks and taffetas prized across the Mediterranean.

advances.name: Diplomatic Mastery
advances.text: Centuries of navigating between powerful neighbors have made Andalusi diplomats masters of the art of survival through negotiation.

advances.name: Keys of the Strait
advances.text: Algeciras, Gibraltar, Tarifa and Ceuta are the keys of the Strait. Whoever garrisons them decides which ships pass between the two seas and what they pay for it.

advances.name: Alhambra Legacy
advances.text: The architectural tradition of the Alhambra inspires a flowering of Islamic art and architecture across Al-Andalus.

event.title: The Splendor of the Alhambra
event.text:
High above the city of Granada, against the backdrop of the Sierra Nevada, the Alhambra rises like a vision from paradise. Its walls of rammed earth conceal gardens of impossible beauty, the Court of the Lions with its twelve marble beasts guarding a fountain of crystal water, the Hall of the Ambassadors where muqarnas ceilings represent the seven heavens, and the Generalife where terraced gardens cascade down the hillside in a symphony of water and stone.

This is not merely a palace. It is the physical embodiment of the Andalusi ideal, that art, architecture, and engineering can transform raw earth into something that makes the heart ache with beauty. Every surface is covered in geometric arabesques, every fountain is an exercise in hydraulic engineering, every garden a masterwork of irrigation science. The Alhambra proves that Al-Andalus can create wonders to rival any civilization on earth.

options.text: Let this splendor inspire our people for generations.

modifiers.name: Splendor of the Alhambra
modifiers.text: The palace complex of the Alhambra stands as a testament to the artistic genius of Islamic civilization, its delicate muqarnas and geometric arabesques inspiring wonder across the world.

advances.name: Corsair Tradition
advances.text: Swift Nasrid corsairs patrol the Strait of Gibraltar and the western Mediterranean, protecting trade routes and raiding enemy shipping.

advances.name: Waqf Endowments
advances.text: The Islamic institution of waqf, charitable endowments for public works, funds the construction of hospitals, schools, and infrastructure.

advances.name: Berber-Andalusi Military Fusion
advances.text: The military traditions of North African Berber dynasties merge with Iberian techniques to create a distinctive Andalusi art of war, producing celebrated swordsmiths and armorers.

advances.name: Fiscal Innovation
advances.text: Al-Andalus develops sophisticated fiscal instruments and regulated marketplaces, with the suq at the heart of every city's commercial life.

advances.name: Taifa Governance
advances.text: Drawing lessons from the fragmentation of the taifa kingdoms, Al-Andalus develops institutions to prevent provincial separatism.

advances.name: Centralized Sultanate
advances.text: The sultan consolidates direct control over the provinces, replacing semi-autonomous governors with royal administrators.

advances.name: Infrastructure Renewal
advances.text: A program of public works renews the administrative apparatus of Al-Andalus, establishing provincial chancelleries to coordinate governance across the realm.

advances.name: The Adventurers of Lisbon
advances.text: Al-Idrisi tells of a company of Lisbon men, the Adventurers, who fitted out a ship for the Sea of Darkness and came home with word of islands. Andalusi yards now build for the ocean, and their ships stay out longer and are refitted faster.

advances.name: Standing Army
advances.text: Al-Andalus replaces reliance on tribal levies and ghazi volunteers with a professional standing army of disciplined infantry under direct royal command.

advances.name: Majlis Council
advances.text: A consultative council of notables advises the ruler on matters of law and governance, balancing royal authority with communal consensus.

advances.name: Paper of Shatiba
advances.text: Shatiba made the first paper in the west of Europe, and al-Idrisi wrote that it was sent east and west. The mills on the Albaida turn again, and where paper is cheap, books and the men who read them multiply.

advances.name: Industrial Modernization
advances.text:
Al-Andalus adapts modern manufacturing techniques while building on its centuries-old tradition of skilled artisanship.

Available in: Dar al-Tiraz

advances.name: Modern Army
advances.text: The Andalusi military adopts modern drill, formations, and firearms technology to match the armies of the age.

advances.name: The Nawba Written Down
advances.text: The nawba is the suite of songs that tradition traces to Ziryab's school in Cordoba. Around 1789 Muhammad al-Ha'ik of Tetuan wrote down the words of the eleven still sung, and the music of Al-Andalus is taught from his book in every city of the realm.

advances.name: Urban Renewal
advances.text: The great cities of Al-Andalus undergo expansion and modernization, attracting migrants and merchants from across the Muslim world.

advances.name: Global Trade Mastery
advances.text: Al-Andalus leverages its position at the junction of the Atlantic and Mediterranean to dominate global trade networks.

destiny.name: Destiny of Al-Andalus
destiny.text: With Iberia united under the crescent, Al-Andalus stands at a crossroads between scholarship and conquest.

event.title: The Destiny of Al-Andalus
event.text: With the peninsula secured and our realm consolidated, the scholars of Cordoba and the warriors of the frontier both look to us for direction. The path we chose at our founding now begins to bear fruit. Whether through the spread of knowledge or the march of armies, Al-Andalus will make its mark upon the world.

destiny.name: The Knowledge Restored
destiny.text: Rebuild Cordoba's legendary libraries and attract scholars from across the world. Requires a library in three cities of the realm, silk in the capital market, and 1,000 gold.

children.text: Silk is produced in the market
Silk is traded in the market

event.title: The Knowledge Restored
event.text: The great libraries of Cordoba are being rebuilt. Scholars from Baghdad to Byzantium journey to our courts, drawn by the promise of patronage and the freedom to pursue truth wherever it leads. The banking houses of Al-Andalus fund expeditions to recover lost manuscripts, while silk merchants carry not only cloth but ideas along the trade routes. The intellectual tradition that once made this land the wonder of the world is being reborn.

options.text: Let the lamps of learning burn bright once more.

destiny.name: Bridge of Civilizations
destiny.text: Extend Andalusi intellectual influence into Occitania, and build up Toledo, where Arabic learning was once put into Latin, as the city of the translators. Requires ownership of Toulouse, a library in Toledo, Toledo at 39 development, and 2,000 gold.

conditions.text: We own Toledo and it has a Library
We own Toledo and its development is at least 39

event.title: The Bridge of Civilizations
event.text:
Our scholars have established a presence in Toulouse and the cities of Occitania, creating a corridor of intellectual exchange between the Islamic and Christian worlds. Arabic texts on astronomy, medicine, and philosophy flow northward, while European innovations in engineering and navigation flow south. Al-Andalus stands as the indispensable bridge between civilizations.

But this bridge can be used in different ways. Some argue we should leverage our position as translators and mediators to extend our diplomatic influence, absorbing the peoples we encounter into our cosmopolitan civilization. Others say we should use this moment to invest in the arts and beautification of our realm, making Al-Andalus a paradise that the world envies.

options.text: We shall be the bridge that connects all peoples.

modifiers.name: Intellectual Bridge
modifiers.text: Al-Andalus serves as the intellectual bridge between civilizations, its scholars translating and transmitting knowledge that reshapes the world.

options.text: Let us build a paradise worthy of our learning.

modifiers.name: Patron of the Arts
modifiers.text: Royal patronage transforms Al-Andalus into a paradise of architecture, poetry, and music, though such refinement comes at the cost of martial vigor.

destiny.name: The Second Golden Age
destiny.text: Surpass even the Caliphate of Cordoba by building a universal civilization spanning the Mediterranean. Cordoba was the greatest city of the west under the caliphs, and is made so again, with as many schools across the realm as al-Hakam opened in his capital. Requires ownership of Palermo, a Kuttab or a Madrasa in 27 places, prestige of 75, 3,000 gold, and Cordoba at 64 development.

conditions.text: We own Cordoba and its development is at least 64

event.title: The Second Golden Age
event.text:
It is done. From the pillars of Cordoba to the mosaics of Palermo, from the vineyards of Toulouse to the libraries of Valencia, Al-Andalus has built a civilization that rivals the greatest the world has ever known. Our scholars have not merely preserved ancient knowledge. They have surpassed it, making discoveries in optics, chemistry, and medicine that the ancients never dreamed of.

The question now is how to crown this achievement. Shall we formalize our academies into a universal institution of learning, open to all faiths and nations, that will shape the intellectual future of humanity? Or shall we turn inward, perfecting the gardens and palaces of our realm until Al-Andalus itself becomes a work of art, a paradise on earth that inspires wonder for a thousand years?

options.text: Found the Universal Academy of Sciences.

modifiers.name: Universal Academy
modifiers.text: The Universal Academy of Al-Andalus draws scholars and diplomats from across the known world, extending the realm's influence through knowledge.

options.text: Build the Garden of Earthly Paradise.

modifiers.name: Garden of Paradise
modifiers.text: The gardens, palaces, and libraries of Al-Andalus have become a paradise on earth, attracting wealth and talent while breeding complacency in the ranks.

destiny.name: The Maghreb Reclaimed
destiny.text: Cross the strait and reclaim the Maghreb for Al-Andalus. Requires ownership of Fez and Tlemcen, and an army of 30,000.

event.title: The Maghreb Reclaimed
event.text: The armies of Al-Andalus have crossed the strait and planted the banner in Fez and Tlemcen. The same route the Almoravids and Almohads once took northward to rescue Muslim Iberia has now been reversed, the Andalusis have come south to unite the Maghreb under their rule. The Berber tribes who once provided the shock cavalry of Iberian Islam now swear allegiance to the Sultan in Cordoba. The western Mediterranean begins to take on the character of an Andalusi lake.

options.text: The strait is ours. Let us press onward.

destiny.name: The Caliphate Restored
destiny.text: Unite the western Islamic world under the banner of Al-Andalus. Requires ownership of Tunis and Marrakesh, an army of 50,000, and prestige of 50.

event.title: The Caliphate Restored
event.text:
From Marrakesh to Tunis, from the Atlas Mountains to the shores of Iberia, the western Islamic world is united under the banner of Al-Andalus. What the Umayyads began in Cordoba, what the Almohads attempted from Marrakesh, has finally been achieved, a single caliphate ruling over all the lands of the Muslim West.

But the character of this caliphate remains to be determined. Some urge us to channel the fervor of our ghazi warriors, maintaining the martial spirit that won us this empire and preparing for further conquests. Others counsel consolidation, extracting tribute from our vast domains and building the administrative apparatus needed to govern an empire of this size.

options.text: The sword of the faith is never sheathed.

modifiers.name: Ghazi Fervor
modifiers.text: The martial spirit of the ghazi warriors burns bright across the caliphate, inspiring soldiers and sailors alike to deeds of valor.

options.text: Let the wealth of empire flow to our treasury.

modifiers.name: Imperial Tribute
modifiers.text: The vast domains of the caliphate yield tribute in gold and soldiers, funding further expansion and securing the frontiers.

destiny.name: Empire of the Crescent
destiny.text: Build an empire stretching from the Atlantic to the Nile. Requires ownership of Tripoli and Cairo, an army of 75,000, prestige of 75, and 3,000 gold.

event.title: Empire of the Crescent
event.text:
The banner of Al-Andalus flies over Cairo. The pyramids and the Alhambra, the libraries of Cordoba and the mosques of Kairouan, the straits of Gibraltar and the mouth of the Nile: all are united under a single sultan. Not since the early Umayyads has any Muslim ruler commanded such a vast and diverse empire in the west.

How shall we rule this empire? As the Sultan of Sultans, a military hegemon whose armies can march from the Atlantic to the Red Sea? Or as the Western Caliph, a maritime power whose fleets command the Mediterranean and whose diplomatic reach extends to every port from Lisbon to Alexandria?

options.text: We are the Sultan of Sultans.

modifiers.name: Sultan of Sultans
modifiers.text: The Sultan of Al-Andalus commands the mightiest army in the western world, projecting power across vast distances with disciplined initiative.

modifiers.name: Western Caliphate
modifiers.text: The Western Caliphate commands the Mediterranean through naval supremacy and efficient absorption of conquered territories.

units.name: Zanata Light Horse
units.text: Berber riders of the Zanata tribes and the Andalusis who ride as they do, with javelins and the leather adarga shield. They wheel, throw and turn away before a mailed line can close.

units.name: Zenata Horse Guard
units.text: Elite heavy cavalry drawn from the Zenata Berber tribes, armored and disciplined shock troops who form the core of the Andalusi mounted arm.

units.name: Ghazi
units.text: Frontier holy warriors of Al-Andalus who fight for the faith, combining religious zeal with deadly skill at arms in rough terrain.

units.name: Nizam al-Jadid
units.text: Modernized professional infantry drilled in European techniques, forming the backbone of the reformed Andalusi standing army.

units.name: Andalusi War Galley
units.text: Mediterranean war galley built in the dar al-sina'a of Almeria, larger and faster than standard galleys, designed for control of the western Mediterranean.

units.name: Nasrid Corsair
units.text: Swift light raiding vessel of the Nasrid naval tradition, designed to hunt merchant shipping and protect the Strait of Gibraltar.

buildings.name: Kuttab
buildings.text: A school beside the mosque where a salaried master teaches the children of the quarter to read, write and recite, without fee for the poor.

buildings.name: Acequia
buildings.text: A sophisticated irrigation canal system bringing water from mountain streams to fields and gardens, enabling intensive agriculture.

buildings.name: Alcazar
buildings.text: A fortified palace complex serving as both administrative center and defensive stronghold, built in the distinctive Andalusi style.

buildings.name: Dar al-Tiraz
buildings.text: A royal textile workshop producing the finest silk fabrics in Europe, taffetas, damasks, and brocades prized across the Mediterranean.

buildings.name: Notaries' Row
buildings.text: The shops beside the great mosque where sworn notaries draw up partnerships, sales and freight contracts in the forms set down by Ibn al-Attar of Cordoba.

buildings.name: Ribat
buildings.text: A frontier fortress-monastery combining military defense with religious devotion, housing warriors pledged to defend the borders of Islam.

buildings.name: Hammam
buildings.text: A public bathhouse providing hygiene, socializing, and ritual purification, a cornerstone of Andalusi urban culture.

buildings.name: Dar al-Sina'a
buildings.text: A state naval arsenal producing war galleys and merchant vessels, the backbone of Andalusi maritime power.

buildings.name: Waqf Foundation
buildings.text: An Islamic charitable endowment funding hospitals, schools, and public works in perpetuity for the benefit of the community.

buildings.name: Lusterware Kiln
buildings.text: A ceramics workshop producing the famous Andalusi lusterware, glazed pottery shimmering with gold and copper iridescence, prized from Seville to Cairo.

buildings.name: Andalusi Forge
buildings.text: A weapons forge in the tradition of Toledo steel, where master swordsmiths produce blades renowned across the Mediterranean for their strength and flexibility.

buildings.name: Suq
buildings.text: A central marketplace and covered bazaar where merchants, artisans, and tax collectors converge in the commercial heart of every Andalusi city.

buildings.name: Diwan
buildings.text: An administrative chancellery where scribes and bureaucrats manage the records, correspondence, and fiscal accounts of the realm.

buildings.name: Bayt al-Hikma
buildings.text: A House of Wisdom in the tradition of Baghdad's legendary academy, where scholars of every faith and nation gather to translate, debate, and advance human knowledge.

buildings.name: Dar al-Jihad
buildings.text: A fortified command center and armory where the caliphate's military campaigns are planned, soldiers are mustered, and horses are stabled for the armies of the faith.

list.name: Hijaba
list.text: The chamberlainship of the Cordoban court, established under the Umayyad emirate and elevated by the caliphate of 929. The hajib stood at the head of his own majlis, received petitioners and embassies, and drafted decrees in the caliph's name. Under Almanzor (978-1002) the office became de facto regal authority. The hijaba centralized administration through the qasr, but at the price of a nobility shut out of the caliph's intimate counsel.

always.name: Head of the Cabinet Promotion Cost Modifier

list.name: Syrian Junds
list.text: In 743 the governor Abu al-Khattar settled the regiments of Syria across the south: the men of Damascus in Elvira, of Jordan in Rayyu (Malaga), of Palestine in Sidonia, of Hims in Seville, of Qinnasrin in Jaen, of Egypt in Beja and Tudmir. The armies of the east were paid from a register. These regiments were given districts to live from instead, and owed horsemen whenever Cordoba summoned them. They served well while the caliph held them, and the same junds backed the taifa fragmentation of 1031 when his grip slipped.

list.name: Qadi al-Jama'a
list.text: The chief judge of the community, paramount Maliki magistrate of Cordoba. Under Hisham I and al-Hakam I the Maliki madhhab became the dominant legal frame of al-Andalus, codified by Yahya ibn Yahya al-Laythi. Ibn Rushd al-Jadd, Qadi Iyad, and Ibn al-Hajj al-Qurtubi all held the office. Maliki rigour bound the realm together at the cost of pressing dhimmi communities into stricter status.

list.name: Sahib al-Suq
list.text: The master of the market. Al-Andalus kept this older title after the east had renamed the office, and it wrote the market's rules down trade by trade: Ibn Abdun for Seville around 1100, al-Saqati for the saddlers and perfumers of Malaga around 1200. Weights, prices and the standard of every craft were set in those books. The office outlived the conquest. Castile kept it as the zabazoque and the almotacen.

list.name: Court of Madinat al-Zahra
list.text: The palatial city built by Abd al-Rahman III from 936, with its Salon Rico for the reception of embassies and its strict ceremonial protocols ranking the entire administration by proximity to the throne. Caliphs received Byzantine envoys, Frankish monks, and Saharan tribute under canopies of silk. Court ceremonial as instrument of rule: ruinous when neglected, as the looting and burning of 1010-1013 made plain. Requires the seat at Cordoba.

list.name: Atalayas of the Marches
list.text: Round stone watchtowers stand in chains along the three marches, each in sight of the next. The emirs and caliphs of Cordoba built them from the ninth century onward, and Spanish still calls such a tower an atalaya, from the Arabic word for a lookout. Smoke by day and fire by night passed a warning down the line: word from Soria could reach Cordoba in about five hours. Villages shut their gates and the levies gathered before the raiders arrived. An unmanned tower was the first sign that a frontier was slipping.

list.name: Count of the Christians
list.text: The Christians of Cordoba answered to the emir through one of their own: the qumis, from the Latin comes, who stood for the community and was held to account for its taxes. A Christian judge beside him heard their cases by the old Visigothic law, and the Jews had a head of their own, a place Hasdai ibn Shaprut held under Abd al-Rahman III. The treasury found the arrangement cheap and sure. Maliki jurists found a Christian or a Jew set over revenue hard to bear.
